summary:
EarthSignal turns NISAR radar data into maps showing changes on the Earth's surface. By comparing two satellite acquisitions of the same area, one before and one after an event, the system detects and measures changes such as a glacier-collapse flood in Nepal, new lava flows on Mount Etna, wildfire damage in Spain and ground subsidence above coal mines in Poland.

The project combines two approaches: a numerical pipeline based on backscatter, coherence and ground displacement, and an unsupervised deep-learning model (UCDFormer) adapted to NISAR data. The results are presented in a web application with a 3D globe, guided 3D tours, before-and-after comparisons, a time slider and an AI assistant.

NISAR radar can collect data through clouds, smoke and darkness, making it useful when optical satellite imagery is limited. EarthSignal makes this data easier to understand for people without specialist radar knowledge, while clearly presenting the limitations of the results and checking them against independent data wherever possible.
details:
EarthSignal uses two methods to detect changes between NISAR acquisitions.

The first is a numerical pipeline based on three SAR measurements: backscatter change, interferometric coherence loss and ground displacement. It uses physical properties of radar data without requiring model training. For slower processes, 12- and 24-day interferograms are combined into a time series to monitor ground movement.

This approach was used to analyse mining subsidence in Upper Silesia, Poland. Areas were considered valid only when consistent sinking was visible over time and confirmed by a second satellite track. As a result, 25 out of 26 candidates passed the cross-check, covering 11.1 km².

The second method is UCDFormer, an unsupervised deep-learning model originally developed for Sentinel imagery. We adapted its architecture and processing pipeline to work with NISAR L2 GCOV and GUNW data, as the original implementation produced too much noise when applied directly to NISAR imagery.

We retained selected components, including VGG feature extraction, StyleTransformer, Fuzzy C-Means clustering and Random Forest classification. We developed the NISAR-specific preprocessing ourselves, including handling missing GUNW data using GCOV masks, physical algorithms, normalisation for VGG input, weighted masking and morphological filtering to remove noise. The model takes two acquisitions from before and after an event and produces a binary mask showing detected changes. The project folder also contains exploratory data analysis of NISAR imagery.

Future development will focus on combining detected changes with land-cover classification. Identifying whether an area contains buildings, trees, vegetation or bare ground could help distinguish between different types of events.

The results are presented in a web application with a 3D globe and guided tours over real terrain. Users can explore before-and-after imagery, figures and explanations of each event. A time slider shows the development of mining subsidence, while Orbit, an AI assistant, helps users navigate the event catalogue.

The project covers four events from 2026: the Mount Etna eruption in Italy, the Ávila wildfire in Spain, the Rasuwa glacier-collapse flood in Nepal and mining subsidence in Upper Silesia, Poland.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Unlike optical satellites, radar can collect useful observations through clouds, smoke and darkness. This makes NISAR particularly valuable during disasters when optical imagery is limited. EarthSignal demonstrates this with a comparison of Sentinel-2 and NISAR observations of Mount Etna from the same day.

The goal is to make radar-based monitoring accessible to local authorities, journalists, researchers, students and residents. The project also demonstrates how NISAR can be used to monitor gradual changes, such as mining subsidence, which may threaten inhabited areas over time.

TOOLS

The project uses NISAR L2 GCOV and GUNW data from the Alaska Satellite Facility, Sentinel-2 imagery for validation and official mining-area data from the Polish Geological Institute.

The processing pipeline is written in Python using NumPy, SciPy, h5py, asf_search, pyproj, rasterio, Shapely and Matplotlib, with Sentinel-2 imagery accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer. The exported analysis pages use MapLibre GL and Leaflet. The deep-learning model uses PyTorch, scikit-learn and scikit-image and was developed on a single consumer GPU.

The web application uses React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL and a custom WebGL globe, with a Node.js backend and SQLite database, and is hosted on Render. Basemaps and terrain come from Esri World Imagery, AWS Terrain Tiles and Natural Earth. Orbit runs on Google's Gemini API in the hosted version and can also run locally through LM Studio with an open-weight language model.

CREATIVITY

To avoid downloading entire NISAR granules, which can occupy several gigabytes, the pipeline reads only the pixels within the selected area of interest over HTTPS. This reduces data transfer and allows analyses to run on a laptop within seconds.

Each analysis can also be exported as a standalone HTML page with a guided 3D flight and visualisations. The application presents satellite data through interactive tours, camera movements and a time slider instead of relying only on static maps.

The assistant accesses only the event catalogue through validated tools and never queries the database directly; its API key stays on the server. The language model can be switched between the Gemini API and a local LM Studio model without changing the application.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We focused on making the results as reliable and transparent as possible. Detected areas are presented as potential changes, not automatically as confirmed damage. For example, the wildfire mask was compared with an independent optical burn map and achieved an IoU of approximately 0.30. This result is reported openly to show the current limitations of the method.

Mining subsidence is checked against a second satellite track and official mining-area boundaries. We also prioritised transparent numerical methods, using deep learning as a complementary approach.

The application includes high-contrast text, keyboard controls and a reduced-motion mode. It uses publicly available data and is hosted on Render's free tier.
projectRefs: Unsupervised change detection using a transformer-driven image translation
